The London Underground is the oldest underground railway in the world.
The first line opened on 10 January 1863.
It was the Metropolitan Railway, and it went from Paddington to Farringdon Street.
The line was about 6 kilometers long.
The first trains were steam trains.
Can you imagine smoke in a tunnel?
But people were not afraid.
On the first day about 38,000 passengers traveled on the new railway.
Today Londoners often call the Underground "the Tube".
It is one of the symbols of the city.
The Golden Gate Bridge is in San Francisco, California.
It opened in May 1937.
On 27 May the bridge was only for people on foot, and up to 200,000 people came.
Cars came the next day.
The bridge is 1.7 miles (about 2.7 kilometers) long.
It was the longest suspension bridge in the world until 1964.
The bridge is not gold.
Its color is called "International Orange".
The US Navy wanted black and yellow stripes, but the architect liked the orange-red color.
It is easy to see in the fog.
On 1 March 1872 President Ulysses S.
Grant signed a law, and Yellowstone became the first national park in the USA.
Many people call it the first national park in the world.
Most of the park is in Wyoming, but small parts are in Montana and Idaho.
It is very big: about 8,991 square kilometers.
Yellowstone sits on an active volcano.
Under the ground the water is very hot.
That is why the park has more than half of the world's geysers: more than 500 active ones!
The most famous geyser is called Old Faithful.
Today tea is the typical British drink.
But in the 17th century it was new.
In September 1658 a London newspaper printed the first advertisement for tea in Britain.
A coffee house near the Royal Exchange sold it.
In 1662 King Charles II married Catherine of Braganza, a princess from Portugal.
She loved tea and brought it with her.
Soon ladies at the royal court started drinking tea too.
It became very fashionable.
But tea was expensive because of high taxes.
Only rich people could buy it, and the lady of the house kept the keys to the tea boxes.
The New York City subway opened on October 27, 1904.
The first line had 28 stations.
It ran about nine miles, from City Hall to 145th Street in Harlem.
The mayor, George McClellan, drove the first train.
A ride cost a nickel, which is five cents.
That evening more than 100,000 people rode the new trains.
Today the subway is much bigger.
It has 472 stations, and it usually runs 24 hours a day, every day of the year.
Many New Yorkers take the subway to work or to school.
For millions of people it is part of everyday life.
London's black cabs are famous all over the world.
But before drivers can start work, they must pass a very hard test.
It is called the Knowledge, and it began in 1865.
Learners must know about 25,000 streets within six miles of Charing Cross.
They also learn many landmarks, such as hotels and theaters.
Their study book has 320 routes.
It usually takes three or four years.
In the exams an examiner names two places, and the learner describes the shortest route between them.
In 2011 scientists from University College London published a study about the brains of learners.
In those who passed, one part of the brain grew bigger.
This part helps us remember places.
The word “pub” is short for “public house”.
Pubs have a long history in Britain.
In Roman times there were taverns, called tabernae, along the roads.
Later the Anglo-Saxons drank ale in alehouses.
In 1393 King Richard II made a law: every alehouse had to hang a sign.
This helped inspectors find them.
Many people could not read, so the signs had pictures.
That is why many pubs still have names like the Red Lion or the Crown.
Today people go to the pub to meet friends, eat and drink.
But many pubs are closing.
In June 2022 England and Wales had only 39,970 pubs, the lowest number on record.
Central Park is a huge park in the middle of Manhattan in New York City.
It is about 2.5 miles long and half a mile wide.
Its area is 843 acres, or 341 hectares.
In 1858 Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux won a competition for the design of the park.
The first part to open was the Lake, in December 1858.
Before the park was built, about 1,600 people lived on this land.
About 225 of them lived in Seneca Village, a community of mostly African Americans.
The city took their land for the park.
Today the park has more than 18,000 trees.
It gets about 42 million visits a year.
The Smithsonian Institution is not one museum.
It is a group of about 20 museums and galleries, plus the National Zoo.
Most of them are in Washington, D.C., and almost all are free.
Its history began in an unusual way.
James Smithson was a British chemist.
He never visited the United States.
He left his money to his nephew, but the nephew died in 1835 without children.
So the money went to the United States.
In 1838 104,960 gold coins arrived in America.
The money was “for the increase and diffusion of knowledge”.
In 1846 Congress created the Smithsonian.
The first building, the red “Castle”, opened in 1855.
Smithson's tomb is inside it.
His remains were brought from Italy in 1904.
The museums keep many famous objects: the Hope Diamond, the Wright brothers' first airplane and the Star-Spangled Banner, the flag that inspired the national anthem.
Route 66 is one of the most famous roads in America.
It opened on November 11, 1926.
The highway went from Chicago, Illinois to Santa Monica, California.
It was about 2,448 miles (3,940 kilometers) long and crossed eight states.
People also called it “the Main Street of America”.
In the 1930s dry weather and terrible dust storms hit the Great Plains.
Many farm families left their homes and drove west, to California, on Route 66.
In 1939 John Steinbeck wrote about them in his novel The Grapes of Wrath.
He called the highway “the mother road”.
In 1946 Bobby Troup wrote a song about the road, “(Get Your Kicks on) Route 66”.
Nat King Cole recorded it first.
Later new interstate highways replaced the old road.
In 1985 Route 66 was officially removed from the U.S. highway system.
But you can still drive on many parts of it.
In 2026 the famous road turned 100.
Mount Rushmore is a mountain in the Black Hills of South Dakota.
Four huge faces of U.S. presidents are carved into the rock: George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt and Abraham Lincoln.
Each head is about 60 feet (18 meters) tall.
The idea came from Doane Robinson, the state historian.
He wanted to bring more tourists to South Dakota.
The sculptor Gutzon Borglum started the work in 1927.
Nearly 400 workers helped him.
They removed about 90 percent of the rock with dynamite, but no one died.
Borglum died in March 1941.
His son Lincoln continued the work, and it ended in October 1941.
For the Lakota people the Black Hills are sacred land.
They call the mountain the Six Grandfathers.
In 1980 the U.S.
Supreme Court said that the government took the land without fair payment, and ordered it to pay.
But the Lakota did not take the money: they want the land back.
Americans celebrate Independence Day on the Fourth of July.
In 1776 thirteen British colonies in North America wanted to be free.
On July 2, 1776 the Continental Congress voted for independence from Great Britain.
Two days later, on July 4, it approved the Declaration of Independence.
Thomas Jefferson wrote the first draft.
Many people believe that everyone signed the Declaration on July 4.
This is a myth.
Most members signed it on August 2, 1776.
John Adams thought that Americans would celebrate July 2.
He wrote that the day should be celebrated with parades, games, bells and “illuminations”.
He was wrong by two days!
Adams and Jefferson both died on July 4, 1826, exactly 50 years after the Declaration.
In 1870 the day became a federal holiday.
Today people watch parades and fireworks and have picnics.
The Hollywood Sign stands on Mount Lee in the hills above Los Angeles.
Today it says HOLLYWOOD, but in 1923 it said HOLLYWOODLAND.
At first it was an advertisement for a new housing development in the hills.
Each letter was 50 feet (15 meters) tall, and about 4,000 light bulbs lit it at night.
The builders planned to keep it for only a year and a half.
But the sign stayed.
In 1949 the Hollywood Chamber of Commerce repaired the sign and removed the last four letters, LAND.
Now it showed just the name of the neighborhood.
By the 1970s the old letters were in very bad shape.
In 1978 nine donors gave $27,700 each for new steel letters.
One of them was the rock singer Alice Cooper.
The new letters are about 45 feet (14 meters) tall.
Who invented peanut butter?
Many Americans think it was George Washington Carver.
But this is a myth.
Carver was a famous scientist.
He was born into slavery in Missouri in about 1864.
From 1896 he worked at the Tuskegee Institute in Alabama.
He studied plants and soil.
In 1916 he wrote a booklet about 105 ways to prepare peanuts.
But peanut butter already existed then.
Long ago the Aztecs and the Incas made a paste from roasted peanuts.
In 1884 Marcellus Gilmore Edson from Montreal got a patent for peanut paste.
In the 1890s Dr.
John Harvey Kellogg created a way to make peanut butter from raw peanuts.
It was for patients who had trouble chewing solid food.
In 1903 Dr.
Ambrose Straub patented a machine for making peanut butter.
So, peanut butter does not have one inventor.
Many people helped to create it.

The bald eagle is a large bird.
It lives only in North America.
Adult eagles have a white head and a white tail.
Their body is brown, and their bill is bright yellow.
Young eagles look different.
They are brown and white, and it takes about five years, to get a white head.
Females are bigger than males.
A female can have wings eight feet wide and can weigh up to 14 pounds.
Eagles eat mostly fish.
They also eat ducks, turtles, rabbits and snakes.
Sometimes they take food from other animals.
A pair of eagles stays together for life.
They build a big nest at the top of a tall tree.
A nest is usually four or five feet wide.
The biggest nest, ever found, was in Florida.
It was 20 feet deep and weighed almost 6,000 pounds.
The female lays one to three eggs.
The eggs hatch after about 35 days.
The young eagles can fly after about three months.
In 1782, the United States chose the bald eagle as its national symbol.
At that time there were maybe 100,000 nesting eagles.
Later, many eagles died.
People shot them, and a poison called DDT made their eggshells too thin.
In 1963, only 417 pairs were known.
In 1972, the country banned DDT, and people protected the eagles.
In 2007, the bald eagle came off the endangered list.
Today there are more than 71,000 nesting pairs in the lower 48 states.
The Fourth of July is a day, when Americans remember the Declaration of Independence.
The story began in June 1776.
Richard Henry Lee from Virginia asked Congress to say, that the colonies were free and independent.
Congress chose a Committee of Five.
The members were John Adams, Roger Sherman, Benjamin Franklin, Robert Livingston and Thomas Jefferson.
Jefferson wrote the first draft.
Franklin and Adams suggested some corrections.
On July 2, Congress voted for independence.
Twelve colonies said yes, and New York did not vote.
Then Congress changed some words in the draft.
The Declaration was ready by the late morning of July 4.
That night a printer named John Dunlap printed copies.
Today 26 of them still exist.
Many people think, that everyone signed on July 4.
This is not true.
The members signed the parchment copy on August 2, 1776.
John Hancock signed first.
In the end, 56 men signed.
Later, people made July 4 a day of parades, games, fireworks and community parties.
In 1870, it became a federal holiday.

Old Faithful is a famous geyser in Yellowstone National Park.
A geyser is a hot spring, that shoots water and steam into the air.
Yellowstone has more than 500 geysers.
It became the first national park on March 1, 1872.
People formally discovered Old Faithful in 1870.
An eruption lasts from 1½ to 5 minutes.
The water goes up about 130 feet on average.
That is about 40 meters.
Each eruption throws out 3,700 to 8,400 gallons of water.
At the vent, the water is hotter than 200°F.
Rangers predict the next eruption.
They post the time at the visitor center, at the lodges and in the NPS App.
Old Faithful erupts about 17 times a day.
The wait between eruptions is often more than one hour.
In January 2025, the middle wait was 102 minutes.
The wait has become about 30 minutes longer in the last 30 years.
Earthquakes also made the wait longer.
Deep underground, the water gets very hot.
The weight of water and rock keeps it from boiling.
Steam builds up in narrow places.
Then the pressure pushes the water out.
The eruption ends, when the water runs out.

Once upon a time, there was an old mother pig.
She had three little pigs.
She did not have enough food for them, so she sent them out to find their own homes.
The first little pig met a man with a bundle of straw. “Please, man, give me your straw,” he said.
The man gave him the straw, and the pig built a house with it.

Soon a wolf came to the door and knocked. “Little pig, little pig, let me come in!” said the wolf. “No, no, by the hair of my chinny chin chin!” said the pig. “Then I'll huff, and I'll puff, and I'll blow your house in!” said the wolf.
He huffed and he puffed, and the straw house fell down.
The wolf ate the little pig.
The second little pig met a man with a load of sticks.
He built a house with them.
The wolf came and said the same words, and the pig gave the same answer.
The wolf huffed and puffed, and the house of sticks fell down.
He ate the second pig too.
The third little pig met a man with a load of bricks.
He built a strong house with them.
The wolf came and asked, “Little pig, little pig, let me come in!” “No, no!” said the pig.
The wolf huffed and puffed.
He huffed and puffed again, but he could not blow down the brick house.
The wolf was very angry.
Then the wolf tried to be clever. “Little pig, I know a field with good turnips,” he said. “I will come at six o'clock tomorrow, and we will go together.” “Very well,” said the pig.
But the pig got up at five o'clock.
He went to the field and came back with turnips.
At six the wolf knocked. “Are you ready, little pig?” “Ready!” said the pig. “I have been and come back.
I have a big pot of turnips for dinner.” The wolf was angry, but he tried again. “I know a tree with nice apples,” he said. “I will come at five.” The pig got up at four and climbed the apple tree.
Then he saw the wolf!
He was very afraid. “Are the apples nice?” asked the wolf. “Yes, very nice,” said the pig. “I will throw you one.” He threw an apple far away.
The wolf ran after it, and the pig jumped down and ran home.
Next the wolf asked the pig to a fair.
The pig went early and bought a butter churn.
Then he saw the wolf and hid in the churn.
It rolled down the hill, and the wolf ran away in fear.
At last the wolf climbed on the roof to come down the chimney.
But the pig put a pot of water on the fire.
The wolf fell into the pot.
The pig put the lid on it and ate him for supper.
After that the little pig lived happily.
